content.text: A function sees the variables of the render that created it, and nothing newer. An interval or listener that an Effect sets up once keeps calling a function from that render, so it reads old state for as long as it lives. Fix it with an updater, a dependency, or, for values you want to read without restarting anything,
Support forwards a ticket: "Auto-save says it saved my reply every 30 seconds, but after a reload the box is empty." The editor's Effect starts an interval that calls
, and it really does fire every 30 seconds. It just sends an empty string each time: the value
had when the timer started, before the user typed a single letter. Someone had silenced the linter's warning about
, because adding it made the timer restart on every keystroke.
The belief: a callback reads its variables when it runs, so a function called by
or an event listener sees the current props and state. If
is in scope, the timer saves whatever is in the box right now.
It's a reasonable expectation, and in plain JavaScript it's often true. A closure holds on to variables, not copies of their values, so a module-level
that keeps being reassigned looks fresh to every callback that reads it. Class components felt the same way, because

was read at the moment the callback ran. And many of these bugs stay hidden: if a value never changes after the first render, the old one and the new one are equal, and the bug waits for the day they aren't.
Every render has its own variables
A function component is called once per render, and each call declares its own
and its own functions. As an earlier article in this path showed, state is a snapshot:
you already have. It asks React for a new render, where a brand-new
constant holds the new text. A function created in the first render closes over the first render's
, and that variable never changes. The closure isn't wrong about what it captured; it captured a variable from a render that's already over. That's a
An Effect keeps the functions it started with

An interval keeps the callback it was given until something clears it. With an Effect that never re-runs, the timer calls a function from one old render for the component's whole life. React's docs describe this exact bug: when an Effect claims it depends on nothing, React keeps using the function from the initial render. Since
lint rule flags it, and the docs recommend treating that warning as a compilation error.
Obeying the linter fixes the stale value but not the product. With

as dependencies, every keystroke runs the cleanup, clears the interval and starts a fresh 30-second wait. Someone who types steadily never reaches a tick, so nothing is saved until they stop for half a minute. The timer shouldn't restart when the text changes. It should read the text when it fires.
Read the latest value without reacting to it

wraps logic that an Effect fires but that isn't part of what the Effect keeps in sync. When it's called, it runs with the latest committed props and state, and it stays out of the dependency array, so the values it reads never restart the Effect:

blocks.title: Not a way to silence the linter

content.text: React's docs are explicit: don't use
to avoid listing dependencies, because that hides bugs. Their example wraps
in an Effect Event called from an Effect with

, and every page after the first goes unlogged. If a change to a value should restart the work, it's a dependency. Effect Events are also only callable from Effects or other Effect Events, never from click handlers or as props, and their identity changes on every render on purpose, so they never belong in the array.
Not every stale value needs an Effect Event
Sometimes the callback reads state only to compute the next state, like a countdown doing
. React queues the function and hands it the latest value during the next render, so the Effect doesn't read
at all and has nothing to go stale.

blocks.title: Pass the value the event is about

content.text: Inside an Effect Event, a value read from the component is the latest one, which may have changed while async work was pending. An argument is the value from the moment the Effect ran. React's docs show a delayed welcome notification that names the wrong room after a quick switch, until the room id is passed in as an argument.
arrived in React 19.2, announced on October 1, 2025. Upgrade
to the latest version too, or the linter will try to add Effect Events to your dependency arrays. On older versions, the updater and dependency fixes still work.
How to apply it in your project
. Each one marks an Effect that may be reading stale values. Remove the comment and read what the linter says is missing.

For every value the linter names, ask the table's question. State used only to compute the next state becomes an updater, a value that should restart the work becomes a dependency, and a value to read without reacting moves into an Effect Event.
